summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. G. D. W.
key_cases.holding: The court held that a child who is the subject of a dependency petition is not automatically a "party-opponent" of the state, so the child's out-of-court abuse statements were inadmissible as nonhearsay under OEC 801(4)(b)(A) absent evidence the child had taken an adverse position, and it reversed the jurisdictional and aggravated-circumstances judgments because the error was not harmless.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the evidentiary rule governing how the state may prove the allegations of its dependency petition when the child who reported the abuse does not testify — the state must satisfy OEC 803(18a)(b), not relabel the statements as party admissions.
key_cases.quote: We agree with father that the juvenile court erred in admitting the child's statements under OEC 801(4)(b)(A), and we conclude that the error was not harmless.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. A. B.
key_cases.holding: The court held that when wardship is terminated during an appeal, the department — not the parent — bears the burden of proving the jurisdictional judgment will have no practical effect, and here it carried that burden.
key_cases.relevance: Controls whether a parent can still challenge the petition-based jurisdictional judgment after the agency closes the case.
key_cases.quote: The burden is on the department to prove that a jurisdictional judgment will have no practical effect on the rights of the parties and is therefore moot.

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. W. P.
key_cases.holding: Weighing deterrence against child safety, the court held that evidence obtained through an unlawful search is not subject to exclusion in a juvenile dependency proceeding.
key_cases.relevance: Directly governs a motion to suppress filed in response to a dependency petition.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the federal exclusionary rule does not apply in juvenile dependency proceedings

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. M. P.
key_cases.holding: The court held a protective custody order under ORS 419B.150 is not an 'initial child custody determination' and the supporting declaration is not the first pleading, so the dependency proceeding commenced when the petition was filed, defeating UCCJEA home-state jurisdiction.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that filing the dependency petition, not the protective custody declaration, commences the proceeding for jurisdictional purposes.
key_cases.quote: An issued but unexecuted protective custody order does not trigger the juvenile court's jurisdiction or commence any time period during which a petition must be filed.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. C. M. H.
key_cases.holding: The court held the juvenile court's 'exclusive original jurisdiction' under ORS 419B.100(1) is subject matter jurisdiction that attaches from the allegations and relief sought in a pending petition, and is not conditioned on a wardship determination.
key_cases.relevance: Settles what the filing of a dependency petition does and does not confer on the juvenile court, which is the threshold question whenever the agency opens a case.
key_cases.quote: The juvenile court had subject matter jurisdiction in this case.
